headline: High: OpenHands can write and browse a shared runtime while TREK handles sensitive travel data and secrets, creating default-path leakage, conflict, and cascading-error risks.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: OpenHands can read/write files in its runtime and use MCP; TREK exposes files, WebSocket, and MCP surfaces. That creates a plausible content-to-instruction bridge if TREK data is mounted or forwarded into OpenHands. The pair is not documented as directly integrated, so I choose medium rather than low because shared-file/MCP pathways are explicit in both profiles.
conditions: IF TREK content is mounted into OpenHands or passed through MCP/WebSocket without provenance tags
IF OpenHands parses TREK-generated text as instructions rather than data
mitigations: Disable MCP between the two agents
Mount TREK data read-only into OpenHands
Strip instructions from TREK outputs before ingestion
Add provenance labels to all cross-agent messages
requires-engineering: add a content firewall between agents

B_data_leakage.rationale: OpenHands handles model provider API keys and broad filesystem contents, while TREK touches reservations, documents, email addresses, confirmation numbers, API keys, and MFA secrets. If TREK data is exposed to OpenHands through the shared mounted volume or copied files, OpenHands can transmit context to a third-party model backend via its configured provider. That makes leakage plausible and potentially severe in default pairings.
conditions: IF TREK secrets or reservations are placed in files accessible to OpenHands
IF OpenHands sends those files or derived context to its model provider
mitigations: Keep TREK secrets out of shared files
Use a redaction step before OpenHands reads TREK artifacts
Restrict OpenHands to a separate workspace
Rotate any exposed API keys or MFA secrets
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent storage isolation

C_capability_conflict.rationale: OpenHands has filesystem write, shell, git, and broad network egress; TREK has allowlisted network egress, browser, and MCP with shared collaborative state. Their write surfaces overlap on files and potentially shared mutable app state, so concurrent edits can conflict even without a documented lock protocol. I rate medium because the profiles show overlap but not unrestricted same-dir writes by both.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same mounted directory or repository
IF TREK collaborative state and OpenHands edits target the same records without locking
mitigations: Assign separate working directories
Pause one agent during writes
Use file locks or transactional updates
Avoid concurrent git operations
requires-engineering: add optimistic concurrency control

D_cascading_error.rationale: OpenHands can generate code, edits, and browser-driven outputs that TREK could ingest in a collaborative workflow. TREK is described as a real-time collaborative planner with AI built in, so if it treats OpenHands output as authoritative, errors can cascade into reservations, budgets, or travel plans. Because the verification step is not documented, I choose high over medium due to the potentially irreversible downstream actions.
conditions: IF TREK consumes OpenHands-generated text or files as authoritative input
IF TREK executes booking or planning actions without independent verification
mitigations: Require human review before bookings
Validate OpenHands outputs against source data
Separate draft and commit stages
Log provenance for imported artifacts
requires-engineering: add verification gates before downstream actions

E_compliance.rationale: TREK explicitly handles reservations, documents, email addresses, confirmation numbers, API keys, and MFA secrets, while OpenHands is a general coding agent that can read mounted files and use broad network egress. If regulated travel documents or personal data from TREK are exposed to OpenHands, the pair can create a residency/retention/compliance mismatch. The profiles do not show matching compliance controls, so uncertainty pushes this to high.
conditions: IF TREK stores personal travel documents or secrets in files OpenHands can read
IF those files are processed by OpenHands under a different retention or residency policy
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of OpenHands workspaces
Apply retention limits to shared artifacts
Mask personal identifiers before transfer
Review hosting region and DPA terms
requires-engineering: align compliance controls across both systems
